newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain unions, employers unveil labour reforms.
newsitem.headline: Spain unions, employers unveil labour reforms.

text.p: Spanish unions and employers unveiled long-awaited proposals for labour reforms on Wednesday, but analysts fear the reforms are not enough to cut a towering unemployment rate.
After months of intense talks, which at times verged on collapse, the year-old conservative government greeted the reforms with open arms.
"I am sure these reforms will end the abuse of temporary contracts and provide more stable jobs," Labour Minister Javier Arenas said.
The government hopes the reforms will go part of the way toward liberalising Spain's rigid labour market, a legacy of fascist dictator Francisco Franco who died in 1975.
They are also designed to prepare the economy for European economic and monetary union (EMU) and reduce unemployment, which is the highest in Europe at just under 22 percent.
But analysts were sceptical.

"It hasn't gone to the root: the reform will not avoid the rigidities of the Spanish labour market and will not make our unemployment fall..The impact will be minor," said Antonio Villarroya, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
Unions and employers reached a preliminary agreement in March which provided the foundations for a final accord, and have been putting the agreement down on paper since then.

The key feature of the accord is a package of contracts aimed at providing more stability in the labour market. The centrepiece is a permanent contract with cheaper severance pay -- a key demand of employers.
Employers had complained that Spain's dismissal costs, among the highest in Europe, dissuaded them from taking on staff under permanent contracts.
This led to a proliferation of temporary contracts, which last year accounted for 96 percent of new jobs, according to the Labour Ministry.

Under the new permanent contract, employers will be required to pay unfair dismissal costs of 33 days's pay per year worked, rather than the current 45, with a maximum of 24 months, instead of 42 months.
With this permanent contract and a reduced number of temporary contracts available to employers, unions are confident a greater degree of stability will be injected into the market.
"This is a serious contribution to the improvement of jobs, as well as to the quantity and quality of jobs," Antonio Gutierrez, secretary general of the Workers' Commissions union (CCOO) said.
Among other reforms, unions and employers also clarified the reasons that an employer can give for redundancies. These include economic, technical, productive or organisational reasons.

Employers had previously protested that the reasons were obscure and dismissal cases often ended up in court. In the majority of cases the judge ruled in favour of the employee, forcing employers to pay the higher unfair dismissal costs.
But analysts doubt the reforms will relax Spain's labour market, which remains rigid despite reforms in 1984 and 1994.
"It will be partly effective ...However it isn't enough, but the unions and employers could not go further by themselves," said Juan Perez Campanero of Banco Santander in Madrid.

Analysts pointed out that Spain must relax the labour market before it joins EMU as afterwards the government will no longer be able to devalue the peseta to help to boost the economy and create jobs.
Unions and employers will present the deal for approval by their executive bodies later in April. The deal is expected to be signed at the end of the month.
